transcript:
This message comes from Capital One with the Venture X Card.
Earn unlimited double miles and a $300 annual Capital One travel credit.
Capital One.
What's in your wallet?
Terms of fly.
Details at CapitalOne.com.
This is NPR News Now.
The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News, I'm Lakshmi Singh.
Invidia shares are soaring up more than 30% this hour and leading a Wall Street rally.
Hours after the company's board of directors did a U-turn and reinstated Jensen Wong as
CEO.
Wong had resigned November 12th following reports of his extramarital affairs, most
notably one with a suspected Chinese spy.
But President Trump tells CNBC he convinced the board to rehire Wong, rejecting the notion
that the Invidia co-founder's reinstatement might pose a national security risk.
"I've been speaking to the board directly and indirectly and I felt very strongly about
it and I felt more strongly as I saw what was happening with the company because that
was to me a very important part of our country.
This represents something very special, what he's done and what the company's done."
Congressman Hakeem Jeffries, the Democrat likely to become the next House Speaker in
January, says Wong's reinstatement is "indefensible."
Wong is scheduled to testify to House lawmakers behind closed doors next week.
Starting January 1st, work requirements are being added to Medicaid, the public health
insurance program for low-income people, and Pierre Salinas Simmons-Duffin reports health
policy experts warn those new rules will increase the number of people who are uninsured.
Right now, Medicaid covers about 70 million low-income Americans.
About 5 million of them are projected to become uninsured because of the new work requirements.
Adriana McIntyre is a health policy professor at Harvard.
She points out enrollment has to shrink in order to achieve savings in the Republican
budget law.
You only save money in Medicaid if you're covering fewer people.
And if you're only covering fewer healthy people, you're not saving that much money.
It's covering fewer people who need health care.
That's where you get "savings" out of work requirements.
Democrats say reversing this policy is a top priority when they take over the majority
in Congress.
Alina Simmons-Duffin, NPR News, Washington.
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky confirms his country's military was behind an attack
that sank a Russian warship off the coast of Libya on Sunday, and PR's Charles Mains
reports the strike was one of several against Russian maritime targets.
The warship Mercury is one of Russia's newest naval vessels.
It was also docked at a port in Benghazi, Libya, home to the de facto separatist government
that enjoys close ties to Moscow when it was hit and sunk by unmanned Ukrainian sea drones.
That strike followed a suspected Ukrainian drone attack Saturday that set fire and disabled
a sanctioned Russian cargo vessel traveling in the Baltic Sea.
Speaking to reporters, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov called expansion of terrorist activity
in the Baltic region a dangerous trend, but declined to comment on the Benghazi incident
directly.
Instead, Peskov referred questions to Russia's military, which ignored the attack in its
daily press briefing.
Charles Mains, NPR News, Moscow.
From Washington, this is NPR News.
Nearly 200 countries are at an impasse after they were unable to agree on how to reduce
planet-arming fossil fuels, and the parties walked away from the COP 31 climate summit
in Turkey over the weekend without an agreement on money.
As Broadway moves into the lucrative holiday season, a local wardrobe workers union has
voted to authorize a strike.
Jeff Lennon reports this comes weeks after union stagehands did the same.
Both locals, which are members of the International Alliance of Theatrical Stage Employees, or
IATSE, have been working without contracts since July.
The locals have been negotiating with the Broadway League, which represents theater
owners and producers, but no agreements have been reached.
A strike authorization is not the same as a strike, but with Broadway still in recovery
mode following an 18-month closure during the pandemic, a work stoppage around the period
from Thanksgiving to New Year's could cause great economic damage and a disruption for
audiences.
For NPR News, I'm Jeff London in New York.
The Cincinnati Zoo has reopened a more fortified hippo cove after losing a beloved hippo named
Fiona to an ingested hat that was accidentally flung into a ceiling fan and ended up in her
enclosure.
The zoo says it relies on visitors to secure their belongings, but in light of Fiona's
death last week, the zoos removed all ceiling fans and added a layer of netting above viewing
windows.
Fiona captivated millions of fans, which began with the survival of her premature birth.
She would have been 10 years old in January.
This is NPR.

topics.text: Nvidia shares surge over 30% after board reinstates CEO Jensen Huang following resignation
Trump says he convinced Nvidia board to rehire Jensen Huang, rejecting national security concerns
Jeffries calls Huang's reinstatement indefensible; Huang to testify to House lawmakers next week
Medicaid work requirements take effect January 1, projected to leave about 5 million uninsured
Ukraine's Zelensky confirms military sank Russian warship Mercury docked in Benghazi, Libya
Kremlin's Peskov calls Baltic terrorist activity dangerous, refers Benghazi questions to military
Nearly 200 countries deadlock at COP31 climate summit in Turkey without agreement on funding
Broadway wardrobe workers union authorizes strike amid stalled contract talks with Broadway League
Cincinnati Zoo reopens fortified hippo cove after hippo Fiona dies from ingested hat in ceiling fan
